summary:
FlameFall is an open-source Python tool that turns microgravity combustion data into fire-safety insights for spacecraft. It trains machine-learning models on flame-spread experiments to predict whether a flame will sustain, and how fast it will spread, from oxygen level, pressure, airflow, fuel thickness and gravity.

It addresses the challenge by quantifying the “hazard gap”: the minimum oxygen needed for fire in normal gravity versus microgravity. It also scores realistic cabin atmospheres, including the ISS and proposed exploration habitats, and produces flammability maps and an automated report.

This matters because materials certified as safe on Earth can behave differently in space, and a fire on a spacecraft has no easy escape. FlameFall gives engineers a fast, reproducible way to find risky conditions and see how ventilation and atmosphere choices change fire risk. The pipeline is tested and ready for NASA experimental data; the demo uses synthetic data.
details:
What it does and how it works

FlameFall is a Python tool that turns microgravity combustion experiment data into fire-safety insights. It reads flame-spread test records (gravity level, oxygen percentage, pressure, airflow, fuel thickness, and whether the flame survived) and trains two machine-learning models. A classifier predicts whether a flame will sustain, and a regressor predicts how fast it spreads.

From those models it computes a “hazard gap”, the minimum oxygen needed for fire in normal gravity versus microgravity. It also scores reference spacecraft atmospheres (ISS, exploration habitat, EVA-prep, low-pressure habitat). It then generates flammability maps, charts and a markdown report automatically, with one command.

Benefits

  • Quick, reproducible risk screening instead of manual analysis.
  • Shows which factors matter most for flame survival, using permutation importance.
  • Works with any data in a simple CSV schema, so NASA datasets can be loaded with a column mapping.
  • Tested (5 automated tests) with continuous integration on GitHub.

Intended impact

To help engineers and researchers spot risky cabin conditions earlier, and to show that Earth-based flammability screening can be non-conservative for spacecraft. The same approach could support fire-safety work on Earth, such as in enclosed spaces.

Tools and technologies

Python, pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn (gradient boosting), Matplotlib, pytest, GitHub and GitHub Actions, and VS Code. The demo slides were built as a PowerPoint file. No special hardware was needed.

Creativity

The project frames the challenge as a decision tool rather than only a data analysis. Flammability maps mark real spacecraft atmospheres, so the output reads as “is this cabin condition risky?” instead of a table of numbers. It also includes a clear path from demo data to real NASA data.

Factors considered

  • Data honesty: the demo uses a physics-inspired synthetic dataset, and this is stated clearly in the README and slides. The results show the pipeline works, not real scientific findings.
  • Flexibility: a standard schema and column mapping so real data can be used without changing code.
  • Limits: tree models give stepped decision boundaries, and the tool is not a certification system.
  • Next steps: train on real NASA data, add uncertainty estimates, and build an interactive dashboard.
projectRefs: UC Berkeley Engineering: NASA-funded project offers new insights into fire behavior in space (background on materials burning at lower oxygen levels in microgravity)
